newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil panel still plans telecom bill vote today.
newsitem.headline: Brazil panel still plans telecom bill vote today.

text.p: A lower house panel suspended discussion on a bill regulating Brazil's telecom sector, but will reconvene at 1900 local time/1800 EDT for a vote on the legislation, an official said.
"We're coming back tonight to vote on the text," Deputy Paulo Bornhausen, president of the Special Telecommunications Committee, told Reuters.

Opposition lawmakers succeded in dragging out discussion of the General Telecommunications Law bill in part due to a motion that voting be suspended until Communications Minister Sergio Motta's role in a new congressional corruption scandal be clarified.
A newspaper alleged Wednesday that Motta may have provided some money to buy congressional votes on a bill allowing President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to run for re-election.

The scandal erupted Tuesday when Folha de Sao Paulo, quoting secretly taped phone conversations, alleged that five members of the Chamber of Deputies took cash for their votes in favor of the re-election bill.

The motion was dismissed by Bornhausen, who said the panel already rejected a similar bid Tuesday when the scandal came to light. But tempers flared during the heated discussion of the motion, causing two lawmakers to exchange insults and nearly come to blows.
Bornhausen said the panel had overcome disagreements among majority members over the bill, which outlines and authorizes the privatization of the federal Telebras system.

He said party leaders agreed to include a provision setting a 49 percent floor on foreign capital participation in new fixed-line telecoms operators, but giving the president the right to raise the percentage if he deemed it appropriate.
Deputy Alberto Goldman, who drafted the legislation, was responding to lawmakers' questions and preparing to announce changes in his text when the session was ordered halted.
If approved by the panel, the bill will advance to the floor of the Chamber of Deputies and then to the Senate.
